newsitem.title: USA: FCC chief close to breaking law, liquor exec says.
newsitem.headline: FCC chief close to breaking law, liquor exec says.

text.p: The chairman of the Federal Communications Commission has come close to violating antitrust laws by urging television stations not to accept liquor advertisements, a top liquor industry official said Tuesday.
"We think he's very close to calling for a boycott," said Fred Meister, president of the Distilled Spirits Council of the United States (DISCUS). "We are watching that very carefully."
Ratcheting up the verbal warfare between FCC Chairman Reed Hundt and the liquor industry, Meister asserted such a boycott would be illegal and that his group would study its options.

DISCUS spokeswoman Elizabeth Board later said that calling for an embargo on advertising "can run afoul of the antitrust laws." Meister made his comments at a luncheon sponsored by the Media Institute, a communications think tank.

"That position is wrong on the law and wrong for the country. The chairman of the FCC has First Amendment rights and so do broadcasters. Suggesting that broadcasters exercise their First Amendment rights not to run advertisements that could be harmful to kids is both legal and responsible," said a source close to Hundt.

Hundt has called on TV stations to reject liquor ads after DISCUS last month ended a decades-old voluntary ban on broadcast advertising. The ban had been in place since 1936 for radio and 1948 for TV.
The beer and wine industries have not had such a voluntary ban and currently advertise widely on television. Cigarette ads have been banned on television for decades by law.
Hundt, whose agency oversees TV station licensing, favours forbidding liquor ads if stations do not abide by a voluntary moratorium. The other three FCC commissioners are divided on the issue.
"Alcohol, in whatever form, is a legal product and should be advertised on television," Meister said in his speech.

"While the current FCC chairman may have forgotten about the First Amendment, I'm confident that several of his colleagues, the Congress and the courts are appropriately sensitive to the vitally important First Amendment rights of broadcasters and responsible advertisers."

Meister said the FCC's chairman's appeal to broadcasters -- given the agency's regulatory powers over the industry -- sends a "chilling" signal. An FCC spokesman was not immediately available for comment.

The agency is divided over how to proceed. The state of Alaska, backed by former U.S. Surgeon General C. Everett Koop, has asked the FCC to ban liquor ads. And a bipartisan group of 26 members of Congress have asked the FCC to open a formal investigation into the ads.
The Federal Trade Commission has opened a formal probe of alcohol beverage advertising on TV, both for liquor and beer.
